query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Limited atomic mobility in solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper HEA nanoparticles preserves local compositional fluctuations, which create nanoscale regions with lower melting points that drive premature surface (premelting) processes relative to homogeneous nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid, equimolar high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (Fe, Ni, Cr, Co, Cu) forming a single-phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Controlled heating of the nanoparticles across the premelting and melting temperature ranges while performing in situ thermal characterization combined with stochastic modeling.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted on nanoparticles of similar size (e.g., <10 nm) and defect density under identical heating rates; comparison with single-metal nanoparticles or well-homogenized alloys under the same thermal protocols.
generation.structural_mediator: Local compositional fluctuations at the surface, maintained by limited atom mobility, lead to formation of segregated microdomains with depressed melting points.
generation.mechanism: During heating, insufficient atomic diffusion in the HEA nanoparticles prevents complete homogenization. This results in microdomains, especially near the surface, that have a locally reduced melting point and thus initiate premelting earlier than the bulk. In contrast, more uniform (baseline) nanoparticles melt in a more homogeneous fashion.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA nanoparticles will show regions of localized surface premelting at temperatures lower than the bulk melting point, observed as heterogeneous melting fronts in in situ imaging and supported by stochastic model predictions. Baseline homogeneous nanoparticles will exhibit a more uniform melting process at a single, well‐defined temperature.
generation.baseline: Single-metal nanoparticles (or well-homogenized alloy nanoparticles) that, due to uniform composition and higher effective atomic mobility, display a uniform melting process without early localized surface premelting.
generation.boundary: This mechanism should dominate in small (nanoscale) particles with limited atomic diffusion, particularly under synthesis conditions that do not promote full atomic mixing. It may not apply if particle sizes are substantially larger or if thermal treatment allows for significant atomic diffusion.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature shift and the spatial extent of the premelted regions may vary with particle size, defect density, and synthesis history, making quantitative predictions uncertain without further controlled studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Using in situ TEM with a heating stage and coupled energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), monitor individual HEA nanoparticles as they are heated through the premelting regime. Simultaneously perform stochastic modeling to predict localized compositional fluctuations and correlate these with observed premature surface melting.
measurements: The temperature at which localized surface premelting initiates
Spatial maps of elemental distribution on the nanoparticle surfaces during heating
Atomic diffusion rates inferred from real-time imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If HEA nanoparticles do not show significantly earlier or spatially heterogeneous onset of surface melting relative to baseline homogeneous nanoparticles, or if no measurable correlation between limited atomic mobility and local compositional variation is observed, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. AbstractThe single-step incorporation of multiple immiscible elements into colloidal high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles has manifold technological potential, but it continues to be a challenge for state-of-the-art synthesis methods. Hence, the development of a synthesis approach by which the chemical composition and phase of colloidal HEA nanoparticles can be controlled could lead to a new pool of nanoalloys with unparalleled functionalities. Herein, this study reports the single-step synthesis of colloidal CoCrFeMnNi HEA nanoparticles with targeted equimolar stoichiometry and diameters less than 5 nm by liquid-phase, ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation of the consolidated and heat-treated micropowders of the five constituent metals. Further, the scalability of the process with an unprecedented productivity of 3 grams of colloidal HEA nanoparticles per hour is demonstrated. Electrochemical analysis reveals a unique redox behavior of the particles' surfaces in an alkaline environment and a potential for future application as a heterogeneous catalyst for the oxygen evolution reaction. reading.lever: Combine stochastic modeling with in situ thermal characterization of HEA nanoparticles to link limited atomic mobility with surface premelting.
reading.why: This approach directly tests whether local compositional fluctuations from limited atomic diffusion drive anomalous premelting in complex HEA nanoparticles.
